content: Shoulder dystocia is a specific obstetric complication in which the anterior shoulder of the infant becomes impacted against the maternal pubic symphysis during delivery. This condition prevents the shoulder from passing below the pubic symphysis without significant manipulation. It is diagnosed when the fetal shoulders fail to deliver shortly after the head has emerged. To resolve shoulder dystocia, various obstetric maneuvers are employed. These include McRoberts' maneuver, which involves hyperflexion of the maternal hips to widen the pelvic outlet, and the application of suprapubic pressure (also known as Rubin I) to dislodge the impacted shoulder. Rubin II maneuver involves applying posterior pressure on the anterior shoulder to rotate it. The Woods' screw maneuver is another technique, which involves rotating the anterior shoulder to the posterior position and vice versa. Delivery of the posterior shoulder, also referred to as Jacquemier's or Barnum's maneuver, is another option. In more severe cases, drastic interventions may be necessary. These include Zavanelli's maneuver, which involves replacing the fetal head into the uterus followed by an emergency cesarean section. Intentional fracture of the fetal clavicle, symphysiotomy (surgical division of the pubic symphysis), or abdominal rescue, as described by O'Shaughnessy, may also be performed. In the latter, a hysterotomy is used to facilitate vaginal delivery of the impacted shoulder. Although the definition of shoulder dystocia is somewhat imprecise, it is estimated to occur in approximately 1% of vaginal deliveries. Recognized risk factors include maternal diabetes, fetal macrosomia (excessive fetal size), and maternal obesity. However, predicting its occurrence remains challenging. Despite appropriate obstetric management, shoulder dystocia can result in significant complications. These include fetal injuries, such as brachial plexus injury, and in severe cases, fetal death. It is considered a true obstetric emergency requiring prompt and skilled intervention.
